paras: The threatened lynching of Pink Pratt took place near Marietta, in Cobb County, Georgia, in late August 1880, when the uncle of a white girl whom Pratt, a Black farm laborer, was accused of raping tried to shoot him as a constable arrested him. The constable took the gun away and lodged Pratt in the Marietta jail, which The Marietta Journal said was done "to keep him from being lynched." The case was reported only in that local weekly, which stated the accusation as fact and later repeated a rumor that the girl had died.

Brit Watkins lived about seven miles north of Marietta, and Pratt worked on the same farm for Charlie Northcutt. According to the Journal, Watkins' eleven-year-old daughter was walking to school on a Tuesday morning, apparently August 24, when Pratt choked and raped her in a patch of woods and threatened her with a knife. The girl told her parents, and Constable W. H. White obtained a warrant.

White arrested Pratt "with some difficulty," though the paper also wrote that Pratt, before being told the charge, offered to go with him "to Mr. Watkins' or anywhere." The girl's uncle, who was not named, then came up and was about to shoot Pratt when White caught the gun and took it from him. Pratt was tied, brought to Marietta and placed in jail.

Pratt waived trial on Wednesday morning, apparently August 25, and remained in jail; the Journal said the girl "fully identified him." On September 9 the paper reported a rumor that the girl had died of her injuries, adding that it hardly thought the report true. No report of an action against the uncle, an indictment or a trial of Pratt appears in the coverage.

The Marietta Journal ran the story on its local page under the headline "A Negro Outrages a White Girl," describing the alleged assault in graphic detail and identifying Pratt only as "a negro man." It closed by asserting, on unnamed information, that "this is the third girl he has tried to outrage," and it recounted the uncle's attempt on Pratt's life without comment. Its September 9 rumor item called the girl one "raped by the negro Pratt," treating the charge as settled.

The same issue reported that another Black man had been jailed for an alleged attempted rape in the county, counted "Four negroes" in jail for that offense, and declared, "This thing must stop." No other white paper and no Black paper was found to have reported the Pratt case.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Pink Pratt
bases: The girl's uncle was about to shoot Pratt during his arrest and the constable jailed him 'to keep him from being lynched' (A1); no one was killed or injured, so this is a threatened lynching rather than a completed one.
All coverage is from one local weekly, The Marietta Journal (A1, A2); no independent report in another white paper or in the Black press was found.

accounts.label: Local newspaper (accusers' and constable's version)
accounts.gist: Pratt raped the Watkins girl and was arrested with difficulty; the uncle nearly shot him, and he was jailed to keep him from being lynched. No account from Pratt appears beyond his reported offer to go 'anywhere' with the constable.

framing.detail: The Marietta Journal headlined the case 'A Negro Outrages a White Girl', stated the accusation as fact, called him a repeat offender on hearsay, and reported the attempted shooting without criticism.
Two weeks later the Journal tallied 'Four negroes' jailed for the offense in the county and declared 'This thing must stop.'

record_check.dossier: Threatened lynching: the girl's uncle was about to shoot Pratt at his arrest, and he was jailed 'to keep him from being lynched'
Rape of Brit Watkins' eleven-year-old white daughter (an accusation)
Attempted shooting (gun aimed, taken away by the constable); no injury
Under arrest by Constable W. H. White; jailed in Marietta; not taken from custody
About 1880-08-24 ('last Tuesday' in the Aug. 26 issue); consistent

info: Alleged assault on 'last Tuesday morning' before the Thursday, Aug. 26 issue, i.e. about 1880-08-24; arrest and attempted shooting the same day or shortly after
Near the Watkins home, about seven miles north of Marietta; Pratt jailed in Marietta
Pink Pratt, described as 'a negro man', a farm laborer for Charlie Northcutt (target of the attempted shooting and lynching threat)
Accused of choking and raping Brit Watkins' eleven-year-old daughter on her way to school and threatening her with a knife; the paper also claimed he had tried to 'outrage' two other girls
The girl's uncle (unnamed), who was about to shoot Pratt; the paper implies a wider threat of lynching
Pratt waived trial Wednesday morning (about Aug. 25) and remained in jail; no indictment, trial or verdict found
